title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Purpose:
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policies, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and the canonical runbook structure. It is intended as the single source of truth for teams owning production services and for SRE collaboration on availability, latency, and cost trade-offs.

Scope:
- Applies to all customer-facing runtime services (hosted API, dedicated control plane, private control plane) and supporting infra (auth, billing, routing, metrics pipelines).
- Excludes purely experimental or ephemeral developer sandbox environments unless explicitly promoted to staging.

Owner and Contacts:
- SRE policy owner: eng-sre team
- Primary contact: Ari Chen (on-call SRE rotation lead)
- Secondary contact: Maya Gonzalez (platform reliability manager)

Summary of Principles:
1) Measure user-impacting indicators (availability, latency P95/P99, correct responses where applicable) rather than internal implementation signals.
2) Set SLOs to balance customer expectations, product requirements, and operational cost.
3) Use error budgets to drive safe change windows and launch policies.
4) Automate detection and mitigation, keep runbooks actionable and tested.
5) Run blameless postmortems and convert learnings into reliability initiatives with tracked outcomes.

1) SLO Definitions and Templates
Each service must publish at least one primary SLO and relevant secondary SLOs. Use the templates below when authoring a new SLO.

Primary SLO template (string to paste into new service page):
- SLO name: <service> availability - successful responses
- Objective: 99.95% availability measured monthly
- Indicator: ratio of successful 2xx responses to total production requests for the API route /v1/generate
- Measurement window: rolling 30-day window reported daily
- Data source: metrics-prod.prometheus <metric_name: service_http_success_ratio>{service="<service>"}
- Owner: <team>
- Runbook: link to runbook page

Secondary SLO examples:
- Latency P95 for inference requests < 300ms (objective 99%)
- Embedding throughput: 500 req/s sustained per shard (objective 95% measured hourly)
- Control plane config propagation time < 30s (objective 99%)

SLO table (example):
| SLO | Objective | Indicator | Window | Alert | Notes |
|-----|-----------|-----------|--------|-------|-------|
| API availability | 99.95% monthly | success_ratio | 30d | page at < 99.9% monthly remaining budget | primary customer-facing SLO |
| Generate latency P95 | 300ms | hist_latency_p95 | 30d | team alert if degraded > 3 days | secondary, user-experience metric |

2) Error Budget Policy
- Definition: Error budget = 100% - SLO objective (e.g., for 99.95% monthly SLO, monthly error budget = 0.05% of requests).
- Tracking: Every service must have an error budget dashboard that shows current consumption, burn rate, and projected exhaustion date.
- Burn rate thresholds and actions:
  - Green (burn rate <= 1): Normal operations. Trusted canaries and rollouts allowed.
  - Yellow (1 < burn rate <= 5): Notify service owner, restrict risky changes (no full-scale DB migrations), require review.
  - Red (burn rate > 5): Stop non-essential releases; escalate to SRE lead; run immediate mitigation playbook.
- Release gating: If projected error budget exhaustion occurs within the current window, automated CI/CD gates must block new deployments unless explicitly approved by SRE and service owner with compensating controls.

3) Measurement, Instrumentation and Alerting Standards
- All SLO indicators must be derived from an authoritative metric source (Prometheus metrics with scrape reliability > 99.9% or Honeycomb traces aggregated). Avoid counting internal retries as success unless they are transparent to the customer.
- Required labels/tags: service, region, customer_tier, route, model_id (where applicable).
- Alerting thresholds:
  - Primary SLO burn rate alert: email + Slack when projected exhaustion < 48 hours. Pager when projected exhaustion < 12 hours.
  - Severity 1 incidents: total service outage impacting > 5% of traffic or cross-region failure. PagerDuty page and mobilize on-call SRE + service owner.
  - Latency degradation: alert at P99 > 2x baseline for > 5 minutes.

4) Runbook Structure and Examples
Every runbook must follow this canonical structure and be stored under /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/:
- Title (short, descriptive)
- Scope and impact (which customers, routes, regions)
- Owner and escalation path (primary, secondary, pager policy)
- Preconditions and health checks (metric queries and thresholds)
- Step-by-step remediation steps (numbered, idempotent where possible)
- Mitigations for safe rollback and communication templates
- Post-incident actions (RCA link, follow-ups)
- Last test date and test owners

Example runbook excerpt: "High inference latency (P95 > 500ms)"
1) Confirm with metrics: run query hist_latency_p95{service="inference-api",region="us-west"} over last 5m.
2) Check GPU pool utilization dashboards: if GPU utilization > 90% and queue depth high, scale dedicated workers by +1 pool via infra-autoscaler (link to CLI).
3) If scaling fails, switch traffic to fallback model variant (model_id: rdx-small-quant) using router-toggle script with safe rollback.
4) Post-mitigation: annotate incident in timeline and add runbook run results.

Runbook testing cadence:
- Runbooks must be validated quarterly. Each service owner must schedule an automated or tabletop drill and record the last test date in the runbook.

5) Capacity Planning Process
The SRE and Platform teams run a quarterly capacity planning cycle and a lightweight monthly check-in for emerging trends.
Quarterly cadence (detailed):
1) Forecast inputs: product roadmaps (expected user growth / feature launches), historical traffic trends (90/95/99 percentiles), model performance changes (token/sec and memory), and planned promotions.
2) Capacity model: use the standard capacity workbook (link to shared spreadsheet) which models:
   - baseline RPS, peak RPS (99.9 percentile), token rate, average sequence length, KV cache hit rate, per-token GPU compute cost, and headroom buffer (default 30%).
3) Decisions: commit reserved capacity for Dedicated (monthly/annual) by region, compute required autoscaling policies, and identify required hardware types (A100/H100/RTX) and quantization profiles.
4) Run capacity tests: execute perf-suite scenarios (from eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) and validate that response time and throughput targets meet SLOs at committed load.

Monthly check-in (lightweight):
- Review dashboards for sustained > 70% capacity utilization for > 72 hours and start provisioning process if sustained.
- Watch model onboarding calendar: new model variants that materially change token compute must trigger an ad-hoc capacity re-evaluation.

Provisioning thresholds (guidelines):
- If sustained P95 CPU/GPU utilization > 75% with increasing queue depth, plan capacity in next 2 business days.
- If sustained > 85% utilization, perform emergency provisioning and consider temporary traffic shaping or throttling.

6) Reliability Initiatives and Improvement Tracks
When recurring issues or postmortems identify systemic gaps, create tracked Reliability Initiatives (RIs) with clear owners, success metrics, and timelines. Examples:
- RI-2027-003: Prefix caching for embedding service to reduce QPS by 20% (owner: Eng-Serving-Runtime)
- RI-2027-011: Reduce cold-start latency for private deployments by optimizing container image layering (owner: eng-private-deployments)

RI structure:
- Title, ID, owner, start date, expected completion, acceptance criteria (quantitative), blockers, and related runbooks.
- Track in the reliability initiatives board (kanban) and review in the SRE monthly reliability sync.

7) Incident Review and Postmortem Standards
- Blameless culture: incidents are investigated without finger-pointing. Focus on systems and processes.
- Postmortem must include: timeline, impact, root cause(s), detection/response gaps, action items (owner + due date), and postmortem severity rating.
- Timelines: postmortem draft due within 72 hours; final postmortem with actions and priority scoring published within 10 business days.
- Action tracking: Action items must be assigned in the task tracker and have measurable acceptance criteria; owners must report status in weekly reliability sync until closed.

Incident review forum:
- Monthly incident review meeting to review sev-2 and sev-1 incidents and identify cross-cutting trends. SRE lead publishes an incident digest summarizing recurring failure modes and top 3 focus areas for the next quarter.

8) Operational Tooling & Observability Standards
Required tooling stack (standardized):
- Metrics: Prometheus for core SLO indicators
- Tracing: Honeycomb for high-cardinality trace exploration
- Dashboarding: Grafana shared dashboards for service SLOs and capacity metrics
- Alerting & On-call: PagerDuty with team-based escalation policies
- Incident timelines / postmortems: Confluence templates + Jira tasks for actions
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions with deployment gates integrated with error budget signals

Instrumentation checklist for new services:
- Export SLO indicator metrics to Prometheus with required labels (service, region, route, model_id).
- Create a Grafana SLO dashboard and link it from the service README.
- Add the service to the on-call rotation manifest and provide runbook links for primary failure modes.

9) Canarying, Rollouts and Safe Deploy Practices
- Canary percentage and duration should be set based on service criticality and recent error budget burn. Default: 5% for 30 minutes, monitor SLO indicators and slow roll to 25%, 50% and 100% if stable.
- CI/CD gate: automatic rollback when primary SLO burn rate exceeds 2 for the canary window.
- Feature flags: use flags to quickly toggle risky features without redeploying; tie flags to testing and canary metrics.

10) Governance, Review Cadence and Exceptions
- SLO reviews: every service must review SLOs at least annually or with any major product change.
- Runbook review: quarterly validation and tabletop exercises.
- Exceptions: temporary SLO or budget exceptions must be documented and approved by SRE lead and product manager with defined compensations and end-date.

Definitions and Glossary:
- SLO: Service Level Objective.
- SLI: Service Level Indicator.
- Error budget: allowable rate of failures within the SLO window.
- Burn rate: speed of error budget consumption relative to expectation.

Appendix A — Example queries and alerts:
- Availability SLI (PromQL): sum(rate(http_responses_total{code=~"2..",service=~"inference-api"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=~"inference-api"}[5m]))
- Burn rate projection alert: query to compute projected exhaustion and alert when < 48h.
